citation.title: On Equivalencies Between Design-Based and Regression-Based Variance Estimators for Randomized Experiments

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] Consider an experiment on a finite population $U$ of $N$ units in which $1 < M < N - 1$ units are randomly assigned to treatment and the remaining units are assigned to control. Denote control or treatment status, respectively, for unit $j$ with the random variable $X_j \in \{0, 1\}$ for which $\Pr(X_j = 1) = M/N$. Reassign an index ordering, $i = 1, \ldots, N$, such that those assigned to treatment come first, $X_1, \ldots, X_M = 1$ and those assigned to control come after, $X_{M+1}, \ldots, X_N = 0$. We observe $Y_i = X_i y_{1i} + (1 - X_i) y_{0i}$, (1) where $y_{1i}$ and $y_{0i}$ are unit $i$'s fixed “potential outcomes” under treatment and control, respectively. [Population moments: p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] Given a feature $v_i$ for $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, we define the population mean, $\bar v$, and variance, $\sigma^2(v)$, as, $\bar v = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} v_i$, $\sigma^2(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)^2$. For features $v_i$ and $w_i$ for $i \in 1, \ldots, N$, we define the population covariance, $\sigma(v, w)$ as, $\sigma(v, w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)(w_i - \bar w)$. [Estimand: p. 366] We wish to estimate the average treatment effect, $\beta$, for the finite population $U$, $\beta = \overline{y_1} - \overline{y_0} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_{1i} - y_{0i})$. [Estimator and expectation: p. 366] $\hat\beta = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$, (2) with $E[\hat\beta] = \beta$, where the $E[\cdot]$ operator averages over all $\binom{N}{M}$ treatment assignments, each being equally likely. [Exact variance: p. 366; stated with a citation to Neyman (1923) and Freedman et al. (1998, A32–A34), not proved in the paper] $V(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(y_1)}{M} + \frac{\sigma^2(y_0)}{N-M}\right] + \frac{1}{N-1}\left[2\sigma(y_1, y_0) - \sigma^2(y_1) - \sigma^2(y_0)\right]$. (3) [Regression form: p. 367 (PDF p. 3)] Define $Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_N \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} Z_1 \\ \vdots \\ Z_N \end{pmatrix}$, $Y = \begin{pmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_N \end{pmatrix}$. Then the regression estimator, $(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y = \begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta_{OLS} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i \\ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i \end{pmatrix}$, (4) and so $\hat\beta_{OLS} = \hat\beta$ (Freedman, 2008b, Theorem 1). For future reference, define $\hat e_i = Y_i - Z_i(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y$, the regression residual. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] The re-indexing depends on the realized assignment: a sum over $i = 1, \ldots, M$ is a sum over the treated units $\{i : X_i = 1\}$ and a sum over $i = M+1, \ldots, N$ is a sum over the control units. The standing condition $1 < M < N - 1$ gives $M \ge 2$, $N - M \ge 2$ and $N \ge 4$, so the divisors $M - 1$, $N - M - 1$ and $N - 2$ are positive. Theorems 1 to 3 are identities in the observed data $(Y, X)$ that hold for every assignment; only Corollary 1 and the two large-sample statements involve the randomization distribution.

canonical_claim.location: p. 367 (PDF p. 3); proof on p. 368 (PDF p. 4)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 1. $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_N(\hat\beta)$. [No hypothesis is attached beyond the setting of Section 2.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Sample variances: p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_1) = \frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1}{M-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(Y_i - \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i\right)^2\right] = \frac{N-1}{N}\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$ and $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_0) = \frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1}{N-M-1}\left[\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}\left(Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i\right)^2\right] = \frac{N-1}{N}\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$, where $\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$ and $\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$ are the traditional sample variance estimators. [Neyman estimator: p. 367 (PDF p. 3)] $\hat V_N(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_1)}{M} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_0)}{N-M}\right] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(y_1)}{M} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(y_0)}{N-M}$. [White estimator: p. 367] $\hat V_{HR}\begin{pmatrix}\hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta\end{pmatrix} = N(Z'Z)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i'Z_i\hat e_i^2\right)(Z'Z)^{-1}$. [HC2: p. 367] Among these, a commonly used version is the “HC2” estimator, in which $\frac{\hat e_i^2}{1-h_{ii}}$ is substituted for $\hat e_i^2$ in the previous equation, where $h_{ii} = Z_i(Z'Z)^{-1}Z_i'$ is the leverage of observation $i$. In this case, $h_{ii} = \begin{cases}\frac{1}{M} & \text{if } X_i = 1 \\ \frac{1}{N-M} & \text{if } X_i = 0.\end{cases}$ The HC2 estimator for the variance of the average treatment effect, $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$, is the [2, 2] element of the resulting covariance matrix: $\hat V_{HC2}\begin{pmatrix}\hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta\end{pmatrix} = N(Z'Z)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i'Z_i\frac{\hat e_i^2}{1-h_{ii}}\right)(Z'Z)^{-1}$. $Z$, $Z_i$ and $\hat e_i$ are in the standing assumptions (p. 367).
canonical_claim.note: Exact identity in the observed data, for every assignment. Intermediate steps printed in the proof (p. 368): $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta) = \frac{1}{M}\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat e_i^2 + \frac{1}{N-M}\frac{1}{N-M-1}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}\hat e_i^2$; $\hat e_i$ equals $Y_i - \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i$ if $i \le M$ and $Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$ if $i > M$; $\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat e_i^2 = \hat\sigma^2(y_1)$ and $\frac{1}{N-M-1}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}\hat e_i^2 = \hat\sigma^2(y_0)$. No finding touches this result. The validator artifact was written for P031-E002 and contains an independent derivation of this theorem in its section 4.

canonical_claim.location: p. 368 (PDF p. 4); supporting displays on p. 367 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement: Corollary 1. $E\left[\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)\right] \ge V(\hat\beta)$. [No hypothesis is attached beyond the setting of Section 2.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $E[\cdot]$ averages over all $\binom{N}{M}$ equally likely treatment assignments (p. 366). $V(\hat\beta)$ is the exact variance of $\hat\beta$, for which the paper gives expression (3) (p. 366). $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$ and $\hat V_N(\hat\beta)$ are as in P031-T1 (p. 367). [Displays the printed proof relies on: p. 367 (PDF p. 3)] Since $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_1)$ and $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_0)$ are unbiased, $E\left[\hat V_N(\hat\beta)\right] = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(y_1)}{M} + \frac{\sigma^2(y_0)}{N-M}\right]$. Subtracting off $V(\hat\beta)$, as in (3), the bias of $\hat V_N(\hat\beta)$, $E\left[\hat V_N(\hat\beta)\right] - V(\hat\beta) = -\frac{1}{N-1}\left[2\sigma(y_1, y_0) - \sigma^2(y_1) - \sigma^2(y_0)\right] \ge 0$. [Bound used: p. 366, with footnote 1] $2\sigma(y_0, y_1) - \sigma^2(y_0) - \sigma^2(y_1) \le 0$. [Printed proof: p. 368] Since $E\left[\hat V_N(\hat\beta)\right] \ge V(\hat\beta)$ and $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_N(\hat\beta)$, $E\left[\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)\right] \ge V(\hat\beta)$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-population inequality over the randomization distribution; this is the exact part of headline claim H2 (the large-sample part is P031-T5). The paper states expression (3) and the unbiasedness of $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}$ by citation (Neyman 1923; Freedman et al. 1998, A32–A34; Cochran 1977, Theorem 2.4) without proof. Whether those pinpoints carry the statements is undetermined (P031-N001), but both facts were checked by exact enumeration and derived independently by the validators. A faithful formalization defines $V(\hat\beta)$ as the variance of $\hat\beta$ over the $\binom{N}{M}$ assignments and proves (3) and the unbiasedness as lemmas; the bias then equals $\sigma^2(y_1 - y_0)/(N-1)$. The validator artifact was written for P031-E002 and derives the nonnegative bias in its section 6.

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 2. $\frac{N-2}{N-1}\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$. [No hypothesis is attached beyond the setting of Section 2.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Hypothesized potential outcomes: p. 368 (PDF p. 4)] By maintaining the hypothesis of constant additive effects equal to $\hat\beta$, we can use expressions (1) and (2) to construct a hypothesized set of potential outcomes, $\tilde y_{0i}$ and $\tilde y_{1i}$, for all $i = 1, \ldots, N$ as follows: $\tilde y_{0i} = Y_i - X_i\hat\beta = Y_i - X_i\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i\right)$ and $\tilde y_{1i} = Y_i + (1 - X_i)\hat\beta = Y_i + (1 - X_i)\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i\right)$. [Constant-effects estimator: p. 368] By (3), the hypothesis of constant effects implies that the randomization variance for the estimated treatment effect should be estimated as, $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(\tilde y_1)}{M} + \frac{\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)}{N-M}\right] + \frac{1}{N-1}\left[2\sigma(\tilde y_1, \tilde y_0) - \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) - \sigma^2(\tilde y_0)\right]$. (5) [OLS covariance: p. 369 (PDF p. 5)] $\hat V_{OLS}\begin{pmatrix}\hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N-2}(Z'Z)^{-1}$, with $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ denoting the [2, 2] element of this covariance matrix. $\sigma^2(\cdot)$ and $\sigma(\cdot,\cdot)$ (divisor $N$), $Z$ and $\hat e_i$ are in the standing assumptions.
canonical_claim.note: Exact identity in the observed data, for every assignment. P031-E002 and P031-A001 (both clarity notes) touch this result without changing it. The first sentence of the printed proof reads $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(y_0, y_1)$; the identity that holds, and that (5) needs, is $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1)$. Two residual sums in the final display are printed as $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e^2$ without the index. The formalizer should prove the statement above from (5) and should not try to prove the untilded equality, which is false (validator example: $N = 4$, $M = 2$, $y_0 = y_1 = (0, 2, 5, 9)$, units 1 and 2 treated, gives $5/2$ against $23/2$). Steps printed in the proof (p. 369): $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{N}{M(N-M)}\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$ and $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Y_i - \hat\alpha - X_i\hat\beta)^2}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\tilde y_{0i} - \hat\alpha)^2}{N} = \sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$. The reading of $\hat V_{CE}$ as the variance of the difference in means over all assignments under the hypothesized outcomes comes from applying (3) to $\tilde y$ and is not part of the theorem statement.

canonical_claim.location: p. 369 (PDF p. 5); proof on p. 370 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 3. Under a balanced design such that $N = 2M$, $\frac{N-1}{N-2}\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_N(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Balanced design: p. 369 (PDF p. 5)] In a balanced design, equal numbers of units are assigned to the treatment and control groups. $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$ (expression (5), p. 368) and $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ (p. 369) are as in P031-T3; $\hat V_N(\hat\beta)$ and $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$ (p. 367) are as in P031-T1.
canonical_claim.note: Exact identity in the observed data, for every assignment with $N = 2M$ (the standing condition then gives $M \ge 2$). The theorem statement is printed correctly. The printed proof (p. 370) writes $V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$ without its hat and $\hat V(y_1)$, $\hat V(y_0)$ for the sample variances $\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$, $\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$ (P031-E002, clarity note). The abstract and the introduction summarize this result as the four estimators being equivalent without repeating the factor (P031-A001, clarity note); the target is the theorem with its factor $\frac{N-1}{N-2}$. The validator artifact derives the theorem in its section 5.

canonical_claim.note: The asymptotic assurances are read within the regular finite-population regime explicitly invoked through Freedman (2008a, Theorem 1), carried by the after-Corollary-1 reference, footnote 2 and Section 4 contrast. A corresponding two-arm formulation has N tending to infinity, M/N tending to p in (0,1), uniformly bounded fourth population moments, convergent first/second/mixed moments and positive limiting marginal variances. These are substantive conditions inferred from that invocation, not measure-theoretic defaults. Positive limiting contrast variance is not a condition of the coverage assurance: D=0 gives coverage tending to one. The finite bias identity and exact HC2=Neyman relation are unchanged. Sample-variance concentration and the coverage deduction must be proved, not assumed from nonnegative expected bias. Both arms grow, giving HR/HC1/HC3 relative first-order equivalence. The W1 M=2 witness refutes a separate normality-only universal contract outside this contextual claim. The archived W2 positive statement additionally imposes D>0 and is a restricted candidate unless its scope is completed. E001 remains a clarity note; no new paper-error target is introduced.
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 367] The Neyman estimator is therefore conservative: its bias is always nonnegative. As demonstrated in Freedman (2008a, Theorem 1), asymptotic normality of $\hat\beta$ implies that large-sample confidence intervals, using $\hat V_N(\hat\beta)$ in a normal approximation will have either approximately correct or conservative coverage. [p. 368, after the proof of Corollary 1] Above, we noted that large-sample confidence intervals based on $\hat V_N(\hat\beta)$ had either approximately correct or conservative coverage. Clearly, this extends to $\hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$. [p. 368, footnote 2] Implications for the other heteroskedasticity-robust estimators (HR, HC1, and HC3) studied in MacKinnon and White (1985) and Angrist and Pischke (2009, 299–308) are straightforward. The other estimators are all asymptotically equivalent to HC2 and, thus, large-sample confidence intervals based on any of the heteroskedasticity-robust estimators have either approximately correct or conservative coverage. [Contextual scope: The asymptotic assurances are read within the regular finite-population regime explicitly invoked through Freedman (2008a, Theorem 1), carried by the after-Corollary-1 reference, footnote 2 and Section 4 contrast. A corresponding two-arm formulation has N tending to infinity, M/N tending to p in (0,1), uniformly bounded fourth population moments, convergent first/second/mixed moments and positive limiting marginal variances. These are substantive conditions inferred from that invocation, not measure-theoretic defaults. Positive limiting contrast variance is not a condition of the coverage assurance: D=0 gives coverage tending to one.]

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Theorem 2, first sentence, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement: p. 369 (PDF p. 5), first sentence of the proof of Theorem 2 and the display it introduces] Proof. Since $\tilde y_0 = \tilde y_1 - \hat\beta$, $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(y_0, y_1)$. Thus, substituting this into expression (5), randomization yields, $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{N}{M(N-M)}\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$. [Counterexample to the last equality of the printed sentence, $\sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(y_0, y_1)$; from the validator] Let $N = 4$ and $M = 2$, so that $1 < M < N - 1$. Let the potential outcomes be $y_0 = y_1 = (0, 2, 5, 9)$ and let units 1 and 2 be treated, $X = (1, 1, 0, 0)$, which is one of the $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ equally likely assignments. Then $Y = (0, 2, 5, 9)$, $\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i = 1$, $\frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i = 7$, $\hat\alpha = 7$, $\hat\beta = -6$, $\tilde y_0 = (6, 8, 5, 9)$ and $\tilde y_1 = (0, 2, -1, 3)$, so that $\tilde y_0 = \tilde y_1 - \hat\beta$ holds. The values are $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \frac{5}{2}$ and $\sigma(y_0, y_1) = \frac{23}{2}$. Hence $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) \neq \sigma(y_0, y_1)$ in an instance that satisfies every condition of Section 2.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Hypothesized potential outcomes: p. 368 (PDF p. 4)] $\tilde y_{0i} = Y_i - X_i\hat\beta$ and $\tilde y_{1i} = Y_i + (1 - X_i)\hat\beta$ for all $i = 1, \ldots, N$ (the full displays are transcribed under P031-T3). [Population moments: p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] $\bar v = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} v_i$, $\sigma^2(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)^2$ and $\sigma(v, w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)(w_i - \bar w)$, all with divisor $N$. [Potential outcomes: p. 366] $y_{1i}$ and $y_{0i}$ are unit $i$'s fixed “potential outcomes” under treatment and control, respectively; $\sigma(y_0, y_1)$ in the printed sentence is therefore the population covariance of the actual potential outcomes, the quantity that appears in expression (3) and that the paper says cannot generally be estimated without bias. [Estimators: pp. 366–367 (PDF pp. 2–3)] $\hat\beta$ is expression (2) and $\hat\alpha = \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$ is the first element of (4).
canonical_claim.note: The counterexample is to a step of the printed proof, not to Theorem 2, which holds as stated (P031-T3). The actual effects in this instance are constant (all zero), so no constant-effects assumption on the actual potential outcomes makes the printed equality true: the hypothesized outcomes are built from $\hat\beta = -6$, not from the true effect. In the same instance $\hat e = (-1, 1, -2, 2)$, $\sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1) = \frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2 = \frac{10}{4} = \frac{5}{2}$, so the corrected sentence (P031-T8) holds, and $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_N(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta) = 5$ with $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{10}{3}$, in agreement with Theorems 1 to 3. The validator's exact enumeration (check_exact.py and check_exact.out, next to the derivation) finds the printed equality false in all 6 assignments of this population and in all 10 assignments of the population $N = 5$, $M = 2$, $y_0 = (0, 1, 4, 7, 10)$, $y_1 = (3, -2, 6, 8, 15)$. To show what the hat missing from $V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$ elsewhere in the proofs distinguishes, the validator also records that the true randomization variance of $\hat\beta$ for this population is $\frac{46}{3}$, while $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{10}{3}$. P031-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). The notes of P031-T3 and P031-T4 call it a clarity note, which was its first-pass class.

canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected proof of Theorem 2, p. 369 (PDF p. 5). Two corrections: $\sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1)$ replaces the printed $\sigma(y_0, y_1)$ in the first sentence, and $\hat e_i^2$ replaces the printed $\hat e^2$ in the two residual sums of the last display. Everything else is as printed.] [Hypotheses] The setting of Section 2: a finite population of $N$ units of which $M$ are treated, with $1 < M < N - 1$. The identities hold for every assignment of exactly $M$ units to treatment and for all real values of the observed outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_N$; nothing is assumed about the potential outcomes $y_{0i}$, $y_{1i}$, and in particular constant effects are not assumed. [Statement] Since $\tilde y_0 = \tilde y_1 - \hat\beta$, $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1)$. Thus, substituting this into expression (5), randomization yields, $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{N}{M(N-M)}\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$. Now, taking $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$ as fixed, $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(Y_i - \hat\alpha - X_i\hat\beta\right)^2}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\tilde y_{0i} - \hat\alpha\right)^2}{N} = \sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$, by (4) and simple algebraic manipulations. Therefore, $\frac{N-2}{N-1}\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N-2}{N-1}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N-2}\frac{N}{M(N-M)} = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N}\frac{N}{M(N-M)} = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{N}{M(N-M)}\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$. [The corrected proof thus asserts four identities, each for every assignment] (i) $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1)$; (ii) $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\frac{N}{M(N-M)}\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$, from (i) and expression (5); (iii) $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2 = \sigma^2(\tilde y_0)$; (iv) the last displayed chain, whose two ends are Theorem 2.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Hypothesized potential outcomes: p. 368 (PDF p. 4)] $\tilde y_{0i} = Y_i - X_i\hat\beta$ and $\tilde y_{1i} = Y_i + (1 - X_i)\hat\beta$ for all $i = 1, \ldots, N$. [Expression (5): p. 368] $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(\tilde y_1)}{M} + \frac{\sigma^2(\tilde y_0)}{N-M}\right] + \frac{1}{N-1}\left[2\sigma(\tilde y_1, \tilde y_0) - \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) - \sigma^2(\tilde y_0)\right]$. (5) [OLS covariance: p. 369 (PDF p. 5)] $\hat V_{OLS}\begin{pmatrix}\hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{N-2}(Z'Z)^{-1}$, with $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ denoting the [2, 2] element of this covariance matrix; the printed proof uses that the [2, 2] element of $(Z'Z)^{-1}$ is $\frac{N}{M(N-M)}$. [Residual and expression (4): p. 367 (PDF p. 3)] $\hat e_i = Y_i - Z_i(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y$, the regression residual, with $(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'Y = \begin{pmatrix}\hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta_{OLS}\end{pmatrix}$, $\hat\alpha = \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS} = \hat\beta = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$, so that $\hat e_i = Y_i - \hat\alpha - X_i\hat\beta$. [Population moments: p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] $\sigma^2(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)^2$ and $\sigma(v, w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i - \bar v)(w_i - \bar w)$, with divisor $N$.
canonical_claim.note: As printed, the first sentence ends $\sigma^2(\tilde y_0) = \sigma^2(\tilde y_1) = \sigma(y_0, y_1)$, which is false (P031-T7), and both residual sums of the last display read $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e^2$, although the paper defines only the indexed residual $\hat e_i$. Sol's smallest repair: in the first proof sentence replace $\sigma(y_0, y_1)$ with $\sigma(\tilde y_0, \tilde y_1)$, and restore $i$ in both $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2$ sums of the final display. The repair adds no assumption and changes no theorem statement; the two ends of chain (iv) are Theorem 2, which is P031-T3, and this target adds the intermediate identities (i) to (iii). The validator's derivation (sections 2 and 3 of the artifact): $\hat e_i$ equals $Y_i - \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i$ for a treated unit and $Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i$ for a control unit, so $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i = 0$; $\tilde y_{0i} = \hat e_i + \hat\alpha$ and $\tilde y_{1i} = \hat e_i + \hat\alpha + \hat\beta$; hence $\overline{\tilde y_0} = \hat\alpha$, $\overline{\tilde y_1} = \hat\alpha + \hat\beta$, both centered vectors equal $(\hat e_i)_{i=1}^{N}$, and the three moments in (i) all equal $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2$. The same finding restores a hat in the sentence that follows the proof, printed as “carries over to $V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$”; corrected, it reads: As a result, the fact noted above that when $N \neq 2M$, $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ may be either too large or too small relative to $V(\hat\beta)$ carries over to $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$. That sentence is a large-sample remark whose formal content is the target P031-T6, where the printed form is transcribed and the missing hat is recorded; it is not a separate target here. The correction to the proof of Theorem 3 under the same finding is P031-T9.

canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected proof of Theorem 3, p. 370 (PDF p. 6). Two corrections: $\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$ replaces the printed $V_{CE}(\hat\beta)$ in the first term, and $\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$, $\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$ replace the printed $\hat V(y_1)$, $\hat V(y_0)$. Everything else is as printed.] [Hypotheses] The setting of Section 2 under a balanced design such that $N = 2M$; the standing condition $1 < M < N - 1$ then gives $M \ge 2$ and $N - M = M$. The identities hold for every assignment of exactly $M$ units to treatment and for all real values of the observed outcomes $Y_1, \ldots, Y_N$. [Statement] With $N = 2M$ and by Theorems 1 and 2, $\frac{N-1}{N-2}\hat V_{CE}(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{2(M-1)}\frac{2M}{M^2} = \frac{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{M}\hat e_i^2}{M-1}}{M} + \frac{\frac{\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}\hat e_i^2}{M-1}}{M} = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(y_1)}{M} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(y_0)}{M} = \hat V_N(\hat\beta) = \hat V_{HC2}(\hat\beta)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Sample variances: p. 366 (PDF p. 2)] $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_1) = \frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1}{M-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(Y_i - \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} Y_i\right)^2\right] = \frac{N-1}{N}\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$ and $\hat\sigma^2_{FP}(y_0) = \frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1}{N-M-1}\left[\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}\left(Y_i - \frac{1}{N-M}\sum_{i=M+1}^{N} Y_i\right)^2\right] = \frac{N-1}{N}\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$, where $\hat\sigma^2(y_1)$ and $\hat\sigma^2(y_0)$ are the traditional sample variance estimators. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement: p. 369 (PDF p. 5), footnote 3] Freedman (2008b, p. 190) gives the exact asymptotic relation between $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ and $V(\hat\beta)$, which depends on the size of the treatment versus control group and the limiting values of the control group mean and average treatment effect. [Counterexample from the validator, to the claim that the relation depends on the limiting values of the control group mean $\overline{y_0}$ and the average treatment effect $\beta$. Part (a) shows that these two quantities can take any values without changing either variance; part (b) shows that fixing them, together with the allocation, does not fix the relation.] (a) Exact invariance, for every finite population in the setting of Section 2 and every assignment. For real constants $c$ and $d$ let $y'_{0i} = y_{0i} + c$ and $y'_{1i} = y_{1i} + c + d$ for all $i$. Then $\overline{y'_0} = \overline{y_0} + c$ and $\beta' = \beta + d$. For each assignment the observed outcomes become $Y'_i = Y_i + c + dX_i$, so $\hat\alpha' = \hat\alpha + c$, $\hat\beta' = \hat\beta + d$, every residual $\hat e_i$ is unchanged and $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta') = \hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$; and $V(\hat\beta') = V(\hat\beta)$. (b) Three sequences of populations. For each integer $k \ge 2$ let $N = 4k$ and $M = k$, let $z_i = -1$ for $i = 1, \ldots, 2k$ and $z_i = +1$ for $i = 2k+1, \ldots, 4k$, and let $y_{0i} = z_i$ and $y_{1i} = a z_i + 2$, for each of $a = 1$, $a = 2$ and $a = 1/2$. For every $k$ and each $a$: $M/N = 1/4$, $\overline{y_0} = 0$, $\overline{y_1} = 2$, $\beta = 2$, $\sigma^2(y_0) = 1$, $\sigma^2(y_1) = a^2$ and $\sigma(y_1, y_0) = a$. Exactly, $N V(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-1}\left(3a^2 + 2a + \frac{1}{3}\right)$, and for each assignment $N\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) = \frac{N}{N-2}\left[\frac{4a^2}{3} + 4 - \left(\frac{4a^2}{3} + \frac{4}{9}\right)r^2\right]$, where $r$ is the mean of $z_i$ over the treated units and $E[r^2] = \frac{3}{N-1}$. Hence, as $k \to \infty$, $N V(\hat\beta) \to 3a^2 + 2a + \frac{1}{3}$ and $N\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) \to \frac{4a^2}{3} + 4$ in probability, and $N E\left[\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)\right]$ has the same limit. The limiting ratio of $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ to $V(\hat\beta)$ is $1$ for $a = 1$ ($\frac{16}{3}$ against $\frac{16}{3}$), $\frac{4}{7}$ for $a = 2$ ($\frac{28}{3}$ against $\frac{49}{3}$) and $\frac{52}{25}$ for $a = 1/2$ ($\frac{13}{3}$ against $\frac{25}{12}$), with the same allocation, the same control group mean and the same average treatment effect in all three. (c) Exact finite instance of (b) at $k = 2$: $N = 8$, $M = 2$, $y_0 = (-1, -1, -1, -1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$, and $y_1$ equal to $(1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 3)$, $(0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4, 4)$ or $\left(\frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{2}, \frac{5}{2}, \frac{5}{2}, \frac{5}{2}\right)$. Over all $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ assignments, $V(\hat\beta) = \frac{16}{21}$, $\frac{7}{3}$, $\frac{25}{84}$ and $E\left[\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)\right] = \frac{16}{21}$, $\frac{8}{7}$, $\frac{2}{3}$ respectively, so the ratio $E\left[\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)\right]/V(\hat\beta)$ is $1$, $\frac{24}{49}$, $\frac{56}{25}$, at the same $M/N = 1/4$, $\overline{y_0} = 0$ and $\beta = 2$.

canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected footnote 3, p. 369 (PDF p. 5). One correction: “the limiting variances and covariance of the treatment and control potential outcomes” replaces the printed “the limiting values of the control group mean and average treatment effect”.] Freedman (2008b, p. 190) gives the exact asymptotic relation between $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ and $V(\hat\beta)$, which depends on the size of the treatment versus control group and the limiting variances and covariance of the treatment and control potential outcomes. [The relation in full, with every hypothesis, from the validator's derivation. These conditions are the validator's and are not printed in the paper.] Consider a sequence of finite populations, each in the setting of Section 2 ($N$ units, $M$ of them treated, $1 < M < N - 1$, all $\binom{N}{M}$ assignments equally likely), with $N \to \infty$, $M/N \to p \in (0, 1)$, $\sigma^2(y_1) \to v_1$, $\sigma^2(y_0) \to v_0$ and $\sigma(y_1, y_0) \to c$. Then $\lim N V(\hat\beta) = \frac{1-p}{p}v_1 + \frac{p}{1-p}v_0 + 2c$ and $\lim N E\left[\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)\right] = \frac{v_1}{1-p} + \frac{v_0}{p}$, so that $\lim N\left(E\left[\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)\right] - V(\hat\beta)\right) = \frac{(2p-1)(v_1 - v_0)}{p(1-p)} + v_1 + v_0 - 2c$, where $v_1 + v_0 - 2c$ is the limit of $\sigma^2(y_1 - y_0)$, the variance of the unit-level treatment effects. If in addition the sample second moments converge, for which it suffices that the potential outcomes are uniformly bounded along the sequence, then $N\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta) \to \frac{v_1}{1-p} + \frac{v_0}{p}$ in probability, and when $\frac{1-p}{p}v_1 + \frac{p}{1-p}v_0 + 2c > 0$ the ratio $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)/V(\hat\beta)$ converges in probability to $\left(\frac{v_1}{1-p} + \frac{v_0}{p}\right)\Big/\left(\frac{1-p}{p}v_1 + \frac{p}{1-p}v_0 + 2c\right)$. The limits depend on the sequence only through $p$, $v_1$, $v_0$ and $c$. No first moment enters: for real constants $c'$ and $d$, replacing every $y_{0i}$ by $y_{0i} + c'$ and every $y_{1i}$ by $y_{1i} + c' + d$ changes $\overline{y_0}$ to $\overline{y_0} + c'$ and $\beta$ to $\beta + d$ and leaves $V(\hat\beta)$ and, for every assignment, $\hat V_{OLS}(\hat\beta)$ unchanged.
